output.title: Measuring late payment terms without guessing
output.body:
If you want to measure late payment terms, keep the decision narrow: are you still tracking due dates, agreed terms, actual payment dates, and follow-up status by memory or spreadsheet, or do you already have a repeatable check that flags overdue invoices before they become a cash-flow surprise?

That is the first workflow worth looking at. Not a finance redesign, just one recurring task: compare invoice date, net terms, and payment date; flag anything past due; and keep a simple log of what was late. If a collection action follows, a human approves it. Money movement stays human. No surprise, no robot with a clipboard.

The practical test is simple. Ask yourself: how many invoices do you issue each month, and how do you currently know which ones are late? If the answer depends on manual review or memory, the workflow is frequent enough to inspect. If the answer is already reliable and low-effort, automation may not be worth adding.

One useful next step is to audit one week of invoices. Note which were paid on time, which were late, and how long manual review took. That gives you a bounded picture of the problem before you decide whether to build anything at all. For a small business, that is usually the cleaner way to start.
